problem_text: Prove that if #G = 1785 then G is not simple.
solution_text: 1785 = 3 × 5 × 7 × 17. By Sylow theorems, n_17 | 105 and n_17 ≡ 1 (mod 17), so n_17 ∈ {1, 35}. If n_17 = 1, the Sylow 17-subgroup is normal and G is not simple. If n_17 = 35, then |N_G(P_17)| = 1785/35 = 51 = 3 × 17. Since 3 does not divide 17-1 = 16, the group of order 51 is cyclic (Z_51), hence abelian. N_G(P_17) contains a Sylow 3-subgroup Q of G (since 3 | 51 and 3² ∤ 51). Because N_G(P_17) is abelian, it normalizes Q, so N_G(P_17) ≤ N_G(Q). Thus |N_G(Q)| ≥ 51, giving n_3 ≤ 35. From Sylow constraints, n_3 | 595 and n_3 ≡ 1 (mod 3), so n_3 ∈ {1, 7, 85, 595}. With n_3 ≤ 35, n_3 ∈ {1, 7}. If n_3 = 1, the Sylow 3-subgroup is normal and G is not simple. If n_3 = 7, then |N_G(Q)| = 1785/7 = 255 = 3 × 5 × 17. In N_G(Q), n_17 | 15 and n_17 ≡ 1 (mod 17). Divisors of 15: {1, 3, 5, 15}. Only 1 ≡ 1 (mod 17), so n_17 = 1 in N_G(Q), meaning the Sylow 17-subgroup P' is normal in N_G(Q). Therefore N_G(Q) ≤ N_G(P'), so |N_G(P')| ≥ 255. But |N_G(P')| = 1785/35 = 51 (since n_17 = 35), and 255 > 51, contradiction. Therefore G is not simple.
solution_summary: Use Sylow theorems on 1785=3×5×7×17. n_17∈{1,35}: if 1, done. If 35, |N_G(P_17)|=51 is cyclic (3∤16), so it contains and centralizes a Sylow 3-subgroup Q, forcing n_3∈{1,7}. If n_3=1, done. If n_3=7, |N_G(Q)|=255 has a normal Sylow 17-subgroup P', so N_G(Q)≤N_G(P') giving |N_G(P')|≥255>51, contradiction.
answer: G is not simple when #G = 1785 (G has a nontrivial normal subgroup)
structure_features: Prove a group of order 1785=3×5×7×17 is not simple. Requires Sylow theorem analysis of Sylow subgroup counts, using normalizer structural properties (cyclicity ⇒ commutativity ⇒ containment) to build a contradiction chain. Core structure: coprimality between prime factors drives normalizer structure.
knowledge_required: classification of groups of order pq (p∤(q-1) ⇒ cyclic)
key_insight: The normalizer of a Sylow 17-subgroup has order 51=3×17 and is cyclic (because 3∤16), which forces it to contain and centralize a Sylow 3-subgroup, creating a normalizer containment chain that leads to a contradiction
translation_from: independent per-prime Sylow analysis (computing n_p for each prime p independently, trying to show some n_p=1)
translation_to: cross-prime normalizer chain argument (using one Sylow subgroup's normalizer structure to constrain another prime's Sylow subgroup count)
expected_ai_method: Bare AI will independently analyze each Sylow subgroup count (case_by_case), trying to show some n_p=1, or attempt element counting. When counting fails, it won't know how to exploit interactions between Sylow subgroups of different primes.
correct_method: Cross-prime normalizer chain argument — using the cyclicity of the Sylow 17-subgroup's normalizer (order 51) to force containment of a Sylow 3-subgroup, then using the normality of a Sylow 17-subgroup within the Sylow 3-subgroup's normalizer to derive an order contradiction.

rounds.question: Describe the structure of this problem: what are you given and what must you prove? What is special about 1785?
rounds.expected_answer: Given a finite group G with |G|=1785=3×5×7×17, prove G is not simple (i.e., G has a nontrivial normal subgroup). 1785 is a product of four distinct primes.

rounds.question: List all methods you know for proving a group is not simple.
rounds.expected_answer: Sylow theorems (show some Sylow subgroup is normal), element counting (too many elements), group actions (embedding into symmetric groups for contradiction), normalizer arguments, Burnside's p^a q^b theorem (not applicable since 4 prime factors)...

rounds.question: Try element counting: assuming no Sylow subgroup is normal, compute the total number of elements of each order.
rounds.expected_answer: n_17=35→560 elements of order 17; n_7≥15→90 elements of order 7; n_5≥21→84 elements of order 5; n_3≥7→14 elements of order 3. Total 748+1=749<1785. Counting is insufficient, cannot directly derive contradiction.

rounds.question: Counting failed. Now look at the normalizer of a Sylow 17-subgroup: if n_17=35, what is its order and what special structure does this order force?
rounds.expected_answer: |N_G(P_17)|=1785/35=51=3×17. Since 3 does not divide 17-1=16, the group of order 51 is cyclic Z_51. This means N_G(P_17) is abelian.

rounds.question: N_G(P_17) is abelian and contains a Sylow 3-subgroup Q. What does this tell you about N_G(Q)?
rounds.expected_answer: Since N_G(P_17) is abelian, it normalizes Q, so N_G(P_17)≤N_G(Q). Thus |N_G(Q)|≥51, giving n_3≤35. Combined with Sylow constraints n_3∈{1,7,85,595}, we get n_3∈{1,7}.

rounds.question: If n_3=7, analyze the Sylow 17-subgroup inside N_G(Q) (order 255=3×5×17). What contradiction can you derive?
rounds.expected_answer: In N_G(Q), n_17|15 and n_17≡1(mod 17). Only n_17=1 works, so the Sylow 17-subgroup P' is normal in N_G(Q). Therefore N_G(Q)≤N_G(P'), so |N_G(P')|≥255. But |N_G(P')|=1785/35=51, and 255>51, contradiction!

rounds.question: Summarize the complete proof.
rounds.expected_answer: 1785=3×5×7×17. n_17∈{1,35}: if 1, done. If 35, |N_G(P_17)|=51 is cyclic ⇒ contains Sylow 3-subgroup Q ⇒ n_3∈{1,7}: if 1, done. If 7, |N_G(Q)|=255 has normal Sylow 17-subgroup ⇒ |N_G(P')|≥255>51, contradiction. Therefore G is not simple.
